message.content:
Electronic music gets **hypnotic** when producers deliberately design *repetition plus controlled instability*—steady patterns, slow movement, and carefully timed subtraction/addition of elements. Below is what key producers and technique writers say, with concrete parameters and direct URLs.

---

## 1. Attack Magazine: Hypnotic techno as layered, evolving repetition

### Dark Cinematic Hypnotic Techno – Attack Magazine

Attack’s **“Dark Cinematic Hypnotic Techno”** Beat Dissected article is basically a step‑by‑step recipe for hypnotic deep techno: layered 4/4 drums, subtle syncopation, and slow movement in FX and ambience.[13](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/beat-dissected/dark-cinematic-hypnotic-techno/)

Key techniques (all from the article):

- **Solid repetitive grid with small off‑grid details**
  - Kick: **4-on-the-floor pattern** on a 16‑step grid using a 909 kit.[13](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/beat-dissected/dark-cinematic-hypnotic-techno/)
  - Closed hat: placed **on the third step of each quarter bar** (i.e. 16th‑note off‑beat accents inside the 4/4).[13](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/beat-dissected/dark-cinematic-hypnotic-techno/)
  - Snare: hits “on the **fifth step of bars two and four**,” adding a light, irregular emphasis inside a bar that otherwise feels locked and repetitive.[13](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/beat-dissected/dark-cinematic-hypnotic-techno/)
  - This is exactly the “micro‑variation” you’re asking about: most hits repeat every bar, but a few only appear every 2 or 4 bars.

- **Layered percussion with motion via modulation**
  - Shaker: a single note on **step nine of bar three** to create a “rattlesnake effect.”[13](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/beat-dissected/dark-cinematic-hypnotic-techno/)
  - Movement is added with **Auto Pan** (“90 Degrees Auto Pan”) and **Vintage Delay** (“A Bit Tipsy”) on the percussion FX to create slow stereo and delay modulation.[13](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/beat-dissected/dark-cinematic-hypnotic-techno/)
  - This is a textbook example of *slow modulation over static rhythm*.

- **Tension by subtraction / restrained FX level**
  - FX like “FX Reverse Glitch” are placed sparsely (11th and 13th notes of bar two) and mixed low (Volume **-10 dB** to **-15 dB**) so they feel like distant events inside a stable loop rather than obvious fills.[13](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/beat-dissected/dark-cinematic-hypnotic-techno/)
  - This supports a hypnotic state: the core loop is always there, while rare, low‑level events keep the ear engaged.

- **Slow evolving space (filter/ambience journey)**
  - Ambience bus: **Ambience Medium reverb** with **Dry/Wet 18%**, followed by “Master Wide & Warm” (heavy compression), then **Glue Compressor** with Attack **0.3 ms**, Release **0.4 s**, Threshold **‑16 dB**, Makeup **+6 dB**, Range **50 dB**, Dry/Wet **35%**.[13](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/beat-dissected/dark-cinematic-hypnotic-techno/)
  - While the article doesn’t spell out automation, this type of grouped ambience with moderate wetness and compression is a platform for very slow **filter or send‑level rides** that change over many bars, which is classic hypnotic technique.

In other words, Attack shows hypnotic techno as:

> Short rhythmic loops (1–4 bars) with steady repetition, plus a few events every 2–4 bars, and slow movement in stereo, delay and ambience.

---

## 2. Claudio PRC: “Constant repetition” and cyclical narratives

### Into Deep Waters: Claudio PRC – Orb Mag

In **“Into deep waters: Claudio PRC”**, Orb Mag describes Detroit’s Underground Resistance as designing “mental tracks with a **constant repetition**, setting up the path of the *musical hypnotism*.”[12](https://www.orbmag.com/features/into-deep-waters-claudio-prc/) Claudio PRC is positioned in that lineage of deep, repetitive techno.[12](https://www.orbmag.com/features/into-deep-waters-claudio-prc/)

From this article and interview:

- **Hypnosis via repetition and minimal change**
  - Orb Mag describes his music and the UR influence as focused on “constant repetition” as the basis of hypnotic effect.[12](https://www.orbmag.com/features/into-deep-waters-claudio-prc/)
  - This is the core of “loop length choices”: typically **4–8 bar loops** where most elements stay the same, with subtle evolving textures on top.

- **Cyclical journeys**
  - The article speaks of Claudio’s “cyclical journey” albums, where motifs return and transform over long timescales.[12](https://www.orbmag.com/features/into-deep-waters-claudio-prc/)
  - In practice this usually translates into very gradual automation curves: filters or reverbs opening over **32–64 bars**, then closing again.

### Claudio PRC Interview – Bunker Music / Home Of Sound / SŪRU

- In the Bunker Music and Home Of Sound interviews, Claudio PRC describes himself as a **“sound creator”** developing “deep, hypnotic soundscapes” built from field recordings and minimal motifs.[2](https://bunker-music.com/interview/claudio-prc-2/) [4](https://www.homeofsound.co.uk/p/claudio-prc-interview)
- He speaks about using **field recordings of water and urban life** to build immersive, slowly shifting backgrounds under stable drum/loop structures.[4](https://www.homeofsound.co.uk/p/claudio-prc-interview)

Concrete production implications from his descriptions:

- Keep drums and core synth pattern mostly unchanged for **dozens of bars**.
- Use **one or two long‑looping field recordings** (e.g. 2–4 minutes, not sync‑locked) that phase against the grid, creating natural micro‑variation in texture.
- Sculpt those recordings with **slow high‑pass/low‑pass filter sweeps** (e.g. cutoff moving over **60–120 seconds**), rather than frequent cuts.

Claudio doesn’t publish precise DAW parameter values in these interviews, so for this part I cannot give exact Hz or dB settings from his own words; the sources stay conceptual.[2](https://bunker-music.com/interview/claudio-prc-2/) [4](https://www.homeofsound.co.uk/p/claudio-prc-interview) I’m intentionally not inventing numbers.

---

## 3. Mike Parker: One sequenced pattern, live modulation, bassline‑centric hypnosis

### TEA with Mike Parker – Tea & Techno

In **“TEA with Mike Parker”**, he states:

> “It’s music that is centred around a **bassline**. I will work with a **sequencer** and I will **modulate that until it sounds right**… Sometimes I’ll spend more than one day on a **single pattern**.”[14](http://teaandtechno.blogspot.com/2012/04/tea-with-mike-parker.html)

Technique embedded in that quote:

- **Single looping pattern as the hypnotic core**
  - One sequencer pattern (often **16 or 32 steps**) carries the entire track; no melodic “song” form.[14](http://teaandtechno.blogspot.com/2012/04/tea-with-mike-parker.html)
- **Continuous modulation instead of note changes**
  - He keeps the notes the same but spends days “modulating” until it’s right.[14](http://teaandtechno.blogspot.com/2012/04/tea-with-mike-parker.html)
  - Practically, this means:
    - Very slow **filter cutoff** sweeps on the bassline (e.g. 200–2000 Hz over minutes).
    - Subtle **resonance changes** to shift perceived pitch or emphasis.
    - Envelope and drive adjustments done in real time.

### Red Bull Music Academy: The Art of Techno Producer Mike Parker

In **“The Art of Techno Producer Mike Parker”**, he says:

> “Just like my music, every single track I have ever made is **recorded live**. I don’t use **multi tracking**, I don’t use a **computer**, I don’t use the **drag and cut/paste**, every single track is **performed live into a mixer** and that is it.”[6](https://daily.redbullmusicacademy.com/2015/04/mike-parker-art-feature/)

Hypnotic implications:

- **Performance over arrangement**
  - The hypnosis comes from **continuous live tweaking** of a pattern rather than editing a timeline.[6](https://daily.redbullmusicacademy.com/2015/04/mike-parker-art-feature/)
  - This tends to produce **long, unbroken takes** where parameters are always in motion, but only slightly.

Concrete usage pattern (inferred from his description, not explicitly numerically specified by him):

- Hardware sequencer (e.g. 16‑step) synced to drum machines.
- Mixer channels with **filters or EQ shelves**.
- Perform:
  - **Tiny cutoff wiggles** (e.g. +/- 5–10% of knob travel) on bass filter every bar.
  - Larger sweeps (e.g. 25–50% of knob travel) over **32–64 bars**.
- Record 8–15 minutes in one take; release an edited section.

Because Parker doesn’t divulge exact Hz/dB values in these sources, any numbers here are reasoned extrapolations, not quotations.[6](https://daily.redbullmusicacademy.com/2015/04/mike-parker-art-feature/) [14](http://teaandtechno.blogspot.com/2012/04/tea-with-mike-parker.html)

### RA Exchange and Fabric article

Resident Advisor’s **EX.761 Mike Parker** describes him as known for “**minimal, hypnotic and beautifully executed sound design** that sits somewhere at the edges of club music.”[11](https://soundcloud.com/ra-exchange/ex761-mike-parker) Fabric’s “Introducing… Mike Parker and his LOST X fabric Mix” quotes him: 

> “For me, techno is something that can be **transcendental, abstract and open ended**.”[15](https://www.fabriclondon.com/posts/introducing-mike-parker-and-his-lost-x-fabric-mix)

Those sources frame his approach but don’t provide practical parameter values; they support the conceptual picture that minimal, repeating patterns plus abstract modulation gives hypnotic, “transcendental” results.[11](https://soundcloud.com/ra-exchange/ex761-mike-parker) [15](https://www.fabriclondon.com/posts/introducing-mike-parker-and-his-lost-x-fabric-mix)

---

## 4. Donato Dozzy & Voices From The Lake: Slowly unfolding narratives

### Donato Dozzy – RA Exchange

Resident Advisor’s **EX.079 Donato Dozzy** presents him as “Hypnotic techno's leading light” and focuses on the parties and contexts that shaped his style.[8](https://soundcloud.com/ra-exchange/ra-exchange-079?in=theo-storesund/sets/intervjuer) The more recent **EX.675 Donato Dozzy** (Dekmantel live) has him discussing how certain albums taught him to build sets by “**leaning into slowly unfolding narratives**” as he moves from one track to another.[1](https://soundcloud.com/ra-exchange/ex675-donato-dozzy?in_system_playlist=artist-stations:83454)

Technique implications from his own words about “slowly unfolding narratives”:

- **Long‑form tension**
  - Transitions, filter rides, and density changes occur over **many tracks** rather than inside a single drop.[1](https://soundcloud.com/ra-exchange/ex675-donato-dozzy?in_system_playlist=artist-stations:83454)
  - In production terms, this mirrors **very slow macro automation**: e.g. a hi‑pass filter on the main pad opening from 150 Hz to full range over **64–128 bars**.

Because the RA Exchange is audio and framed as “songs that shaped his craft,” it does not give explicit device names or parameter values; the “slow narrative” concept is explicitly mentioned, but technical extrapolation (bar counts, Hz examples) is mine.[1](https://soundcloud.com/ra-exchange/ex675-donato-dozzy?in_system_playlist=artist-stations:83454) [8](https://soundcloud.com/ra-exchange/ra-exchange-079?in=theo-storesund/sets/intervjuer)

### Voices From The Lake – RA Exchange

RA’s **EX.787 Voices From The Lake** notes that their guiding concepts draw from **improvisation**, Japanese design aesthetics, and minimalist visual art (including Mike Parker).[3](https://soundcloud.com/resident-advisor/ex-787-voices-from-the-lake)

Hypnotic techniques implied:

- **Improvised evolution over a fixed loop**
  - They improvise on top of repetitive structures, changing timbre and density gradually rather than re‑writing the pattern frequently.[3](https://soundcloud.com/resident-advisor/ex-787-voices-from-the-lake)
- **Minimalist design**
  - Borrowing from minimal art implies heavy use of simple shapes (sine, triangle waves, simple rhythmic cells) and **very slow, subtle transformations**.

Again, this source is conceptual; it does not specify exact bar lengths or device names, so any concrete numbers are extrapolation, not direct citation.[3](https://soundcloud.com/resident-advisor/ex-787-voices-from-the-lake)

---

## 5. General hypnotic techniques tied back to these producers & articles

Where producers and writers converge (cross‑referenced to the sources above):

### 5.1 Repetition with micro‑variation

- **Short loops (1–4 bars) for drums and main sequencer patterns**, repeated nearly unchanged for long stretches.
  - Attack’s 4/4 kick + fixed hat and snare pattern shows this clearly.[13](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/beat-dissected/dark-cinematic-hypnotic-techno/)
  - Mike Parker’s focus on a single bassline pattern emphasizes this on the melodic side.[14](http://teaandtechno.blogspot.com/2012/04/tea-with-mike-parker.html)

- **Micro‑variation via rare events and modulation**:
  - Hats and snares that hit slightly “inside” the bar (third step of each quarter bar, fifth step of bars two and four) create repeating but non‑obvious grids.[13](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/beat-dissected/dark-cinematic-hypnotic-techno/)
  - Parker’s continuous modulation of a fixed sequence is micro‑variation in timbre rather than rhythm.[14](http://teaandtechno.blogspot.com/2012/04/tea-with-mike-parker.html)

Practical recipe consistent with these sources:

- Program:
  - Kick: 4/4 on steps 1, 5, 9, 13.
  - Hat: 16th‑note off‑grid accents (e.g. step 3 in each 4‑step quarter).
  - Snare: only on some bars (e.g. 5th step of bar 2 and 4).
- Keep note positions fixed; automate:
  - Hat volume ±1–2 dB over 16 bars.
  - Bass filter cutoff drifting slowly.

### 5.2 Loop length, polymeter, odd‑length loops

The explicit sources you asked for don’t spell out “16‑ vs 12‑step polymeter” in direct words, but:

- Mike Parker’s emphasis on **sequencer patterns** and the “single pattern” approach suggests fixed‑length patterns (commonly **16 or 32 steps**) against other fixed‑length drums.[14](http://teaandtechno.blogspot.com/2012/04/tea-with-mike-parker.html)
- Orb Mag’s discussion of “constant repetition” and hypnotic tracks implies standard bar‑length loops (4 or 8 bars) repeating with minimal change.[12](https://www.orbmag.com/features/into-deep-waters-claudio-prc/)

Since none of these sources explicitly mention **polymeter or odd‑length loops** (e.g. 5/4 against 4/4) with exact numbers, I cannot honestly claim “Parker uses 15‑step sequences over 4/4 drums” from these URLs. Any such detail would be speculation, so I’m explicitly avoiding it.

### 5.3 Slow modulation

Across the sources:

- Parker: “I will **modulate** [the sequenced bassline] until it sounds right,” which clearly indicates **ongoing parameter movement** instead of static sound.[14](http://teaandtechno.blogspot.com/2012/04/tea-with-mike-parker.html)
- Attack: uses Auto Pan and Vintage Delay specifically “to **create some tension and modulate the movement** of the snake [shaker],” i.e. slow stereo and delay modulation on a repetitive pattern.[13](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/beat-dissected/dark-cinematic-hypnotic-techno/)
- Dozzy: talks about “slowly unfolding narratives,” suggesting that modulation and structural change happen over long timescales.[1](https://soundcloud.com/ra-exchange/ex675-donato-dozzy?in_system_playlist=artist-stations:83454)

Practical approach, consistent with these sources:

- Choose one main pattern (bass or pad).
- Add:
  - Auto Pan at **90°** phase offset, rate around **0.1–0.3 Hz** (one full pan every 3–10 seconds).
  - Filter automation over 32–64 bars.
  - Delay feedback changes over 16–32 bars.

Exact numbers above are extrapolated from typical usage; the sources give the *devices* and the intention (“modulate movement,” “slow narrative”) but not specific numeric values.[1](https://soundcloud.com/ra-exchange/ex675-donato-dozzy?in_system_playlist=artist-stations:83454) [13](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/beat-dissected/dark-cinematic-hypnotic-techno/) [14](http://teaandtechno.blogspot.com/2012/04/tea-with-mike-parker.html)

### 5.4 Tension by subtraction

- Attack’s arrangement keeps many FX and percussion hits low in the mix and relatively sparse (e.g. reverse FX on steps 11 and 13 of bar 2, not every bar), which creates **tension simply by having fewer events and only occasionally injecting new ones**.[13](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/beat-dissected/dark-cinematic-hypnotic-techno/)
- Mike Parker’s “let the track play longer” comment about live sets (MnmlMagnet interview) points to letting one pattern or one track ride for a long time and **avoiding over‑mixing**, which is another form of tension via restraint.[10](https://mnmt.no/magazine/2018/10/14/mike-parker-on-his-live-sets-the-european-crowd-and-the-change-from-vinyl-to-cdj/)

Concrete technique:

- Instead of adding fills every 8 bars:
  - Remove elements for **16–32 bars** (e.g. mute open hat or one percussion layer).
  - Reintroduce them without big volume spikes.
- Use very low‑level FX (‑10 to ‑15 dB as Attack suggests) so tension is mostly from **structural absence/presence**, not obvious big effects.[13](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/beat-dissected/dark-cinematic-hypnotic-techno/)

### 5.5 Filter journeys and space

- Attack’s ambience chain (Ambience Medium, Master Wide & Warm, Glue Compressor) is a clear template for an evolving space bus; with **18% wet** reverb and medium‑slow compression envelope, it’s ideal for long filter journeys over the entire reverb return.[13](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/beat-dissected/dark-cinematic-hypnotic-techno/)
- Claudio PRC’s use of field recordings and “deep, hypnotic soundscapes” suggests **slow EQ and filtering** of textures to move the perceived environment over time.[4](https://www.homeofsound.co.uk/p/claudio-prc-interview)

Practical technique, matching these ideas:

- Put all atmospheres and FX into one bus.
- Add:
  - LP filter sweeping from ~8 kHz down to 2–4 kHz over **64 bars**, then back up.
  - HP filter gently moving between 100–300 Hz over **32 bars**.
- Drive the bus slightly into a compressor (similar to Glue Compressor settings Attack gives) to keep overall level stable while brightness and body change.[13](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/beat-dissected/dark-cinematic-hypnotic-techno/)

These numeric values are consistent with the article’s use of Glue Compressor and Ambience, but the exact Hz points are extrapolated by me because they are not specified in the text.[13](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/beat-dissected/dark-cinematic-hypnotic-techno/) [4](https://www.homeofsound.co.uk/p/claudio-prc-interview)

---

## 6. What I could *not* source explicitly

Per your request, here are items I *cannot* directly back with producer quotes or article text from the URLs above:

- Donato Dozzy, Wata Igarashi, Ness, Refracted: none of the retrieved sources in this turn gave **explicit production‑parameter descriptions** (e.g. “I use 19‑step polymetric loops” or “I automate filter cutoff by 6 dB every 32 bars”). Their RA features and interviews are primarily aesthetic and contextual, not technical.
- **Polymeter / odd‑length loop numbers**: I did not find explicit statements like “I use 5/4 against 4/4” or “my main sequence is 15 steps long” in the sources accessed this turn, so I am deliberately not inventing them.
- Detailed Ableton One Thing / Ableton.com blog entries about hypnotic techno: they were requested but not surfaced among the results I had for this turn, so I cannot cite specific Ableton articles with URLs and parameters here.

If you want, I can next time focus specifically on Ableton One Thing, Sound On Sound, and deep‑dive RA features (especially on Igarashi, Van Hoesen, Ness, Refracted) to extract any available **concrete device+parameter recipes** for hypnotic repetition and modulation.
